analysis.one_liner: Requires payday and online small-dollar lenders to register federally and obey state interest-rate caps.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2024 with 10 cosponsors, the bill never received a committee hearing or vote and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would force payday, online installment, and other small-dollar lenders to register with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau before making loans of $5,000 or less. It would require internet-based and national-bank small-dollar loans to follow the interest-rate caps and fee limits of the borrower's home state, closing common routes lenders use to dodge state laws. It would also ban overdraft fees on prepaid accounts, stop companies from selling borrowers' bank account and Social Security numbers unless they are actually the lender, and let consumers block or cancel unauthorized paper checks drawn on their accounts.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who take out small-dollar loans — typically people living paycheck to paycheck facing an emergency expense. They would get lenders registered and accountable to a federal regulator, protection from high-rate loans that evade their state's caps, and new limits on overdraft fees, lead-generation data harvesting, and unauthorized account debits.

how_it_helps.text: Small-dollar lenders (loans of $5,000 or less, repaid in installments) must register with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau before issuing credit, and the definition covers not just lenders but anyone who brokers, arranges, or gathers applications for such loans.

Small-dollar loans made over the internet, by phone, by mail, or by a national bank must comply with the interest-rate, fee, and charge laws of the state where the borrower lives — targeting the way online lenders and bank-partnership arrangements have historically gotten around state rate caps.

A remotely created check (a payment order drawn on a consumer's account without the consumer's signature) can only be issued by a person the consumer has designated in writing with their bank, and the consumer can revoke that designation at any time; no such payment order may be issued in retaliation for a consumer exercising their rights under consumer financial law.
Any electronic fund transfer used to repay a small-dollar loan is treated as a preauthorized transfer, giving borrowers the same federal protections that apply to recurring automatic debits.
Companies may no longer charge overdraft or insufficient-funds fees on prepaid accounts, and the CFPB can prohibit additional prepaid fees by rule.

Lead generators may not collect or distribute sensitive financial information — Social Security numbers, bank account and routing numbers, account access codes — in connection with a small-dollar loan unless they are directly making the loan themselves, and they must prominently disclose who they are and how they can be served with legal process.
The Government Accountability Office must study access to capital on tribal reservations and how small-dollar credit has affected economic opportunity for tribal members, with a report to Congress.

analysis.who_pays: High-cost small-dollar lenders, lead-generation companies that profit from selling loan applicants' financial data, prepaid card issuers that collect overdraft fees, and any lender whose business model relied on charging rates or fees above what the borrower's state allows. Some borrowers with poor credit who currently rely on payday products might face fewer options or turn to informal sources, a cost supporters of strict rules generally accept as the price of ending debt traps.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday lenders, lead brokers, prepaid card issuers

drawbacks.text: The bill does not set a federal interest-rate cap; in states that allow very high rates, high-cost small-dollar lending remains legal, so the protection depends entirely on where a borrower lives.

Tighter rules could reduce access to short-term credit for borrowers who cannot qualify for bank loans or credit cards, and the bill itself acknowledges the access question by directing a study of capital availability on tribal reservations, where mainstream credit is scarce.

The registration requirement applies broadly to anyone who facilitates or gathers applications for small-dollar loans, which could impose compliance costs on some smaller or community lenders that already follow state rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers, the main effects are clearly protective: accountability to a federal regulator, state rate caps applied to internet and national-bank loans, an end to prepaid overdraft fees, and curbs on data brokers and unauthorized account debits. The real trade-off is access: some people who use payday loans because no other lender will serve them could be left with fewer options, and the bill wisely commissions a study of that problem rather than pretending it doesn't exist. The bill is a consumer-protection measure, not a rate cap, so in states with no caps it does less than its title suggests — but its targeting of the channels lenders use to evade state law is where most of its value lies.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in September 2024 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never held a hearing or markup on it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the Stopping Abuse and Fraud in Electronic Lending (SAFE Lending) Act of 2024 on September 19, 2024, with nine Democratic senators and one independent as cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a committee markup, a hearing listed on its action page, a floor vote, or passage in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
All ten cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Senate Republican cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-cost small-dollar lenders keep operating under the current rulebook, lead generators keep harvesting and selling loan applicants' financial data, and prepaid card issuers keep collecting overdraft fees. Borrowers in states without strong rate caps remain exposed to internet loans that ignore their state's laws.

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized ten cosponsors behind it.

against.name: Sherrod Brown
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill; it sat in committee from referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All ten cosponsors were Democrats or independents — 9 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 independents — and none of the 49 Senate Republicans supported it; the bill also died in a committee chaired by a Democrat without ever reaching the floor.

industries.industry: Payday and online high-cost installment lenders
industries.note: These lenders would have to register with the CFPB and, for internet and national-bank loans, obey the borrower's state rate and fee caps — closing the online channels and bank partnerships they use to get around state laws. Their business depends on charging rates and fees the borrower's home state may prohibit, which puts their interest against the people the bill protects.

The bill bars anyone who is not the actual lender from collecting and distributing loan applicants' Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, and access codes in connection with small-dollar loans, and requires them to disclose their identity. These companies profit from selling sensitive consumer data, so their interest runs against borrowers' financial privacy.
Overdraft and insufficient-funds fees on prepaid accounts would be banned, removing a fee stream charged disproportionately to unbanked and underbanked consumers.

industries.industry: Banks making small-dollar loans, including national banks
industries.note: National-bank small-dollar loans would have to follow the borrower's state rate and fee caps, which reduces revenue on high-rate products, but banks already operate under federal supervision and many offer lower-cost small-dollar credit that complies with state rules.
